<subagent sessionID="ses_e2375f5b6ffeRywIzyoEM0O9Bm" state="completed">
## Highest-impact visual improvements

1. **Make the existing windows actual openings, not overlays.**  
   In `/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/game.js`, `segmentWall()` (lines 77–80) only cuts door openings, while `windowWall()` (lines 125–126) places panes and frames directly over those solid walls. The wall can obscure the glass, and its collider still blocks the opening. Add window openings to the wall-building layout and construct the wall sections, frame, sill, and pane around each opening.  
   **Risk:** Keep the visual opening and collider layout in sync so players can’t see through a window they can’t approach—or walk through a wall.

2. **Restore distinct room-light levels and give the lights visible sources.**  
   `makeRoom()` assigns different intensities per room (lines 82–86), but `updateLightAndSky()` (line 234) resets every room light to the same `.46`-based value on every update. Preserve each light’s configured base intensity and scale it with time of day instead. Add a simple ceiling fixture or bulb near each room’s existing point light so the illumination has a visible source; the existing `lamp()` helper (line 130) could also be extended with a small emissive bulb.  
   **Risk:** Avoid enabling shadows on every room point light; that can be costly. A few prioritized shadow-casting lights or simple contact-shadow details are safer.

3. **Add an exterior roof silhouette while leaving interior ceilings intact.**  
   The room ceilings are flat slabs from `ceiling()` (line 76), but there is no visible roof geometry among the exterior construction (lines 99–126). A small number of simple gable-roof meshes above the room ceilings would make the house read much more convincingly from outside without adding much geometry.  
   **Risk:** Keep the roof above the existing ceilings and check it from outdoor sightlines so it doesn’t intrude into interior views or block intended access.

4. **Improve shadow quality where it matters instead of raising global cost.**  
   The directional sun casts shadows, but its 1024² map covers a broad area (`sun` setup at line 121), while all room point lights explicitly have shadows disabled (line 85). First tighten the sun’s shadow-camera bounds to the house and nearby playable grounds; this should allocate more resolution to the house without increasing map size. If interior shadows are still too flat, test a shadow map on only the most important practical light.  
   **Risk:** Tight bounds can clip shadows from outdoor trees or the porch; verify those views before narrowing further. Multiple shadowed point lights would be the expensive option.

5. **Add restrained surface variation at a larger scale.**  
   `surfaceMap()` (lines 25–34) creates mostly per-pixel noise, and the same texture is used for color and bump on several materials (line 35). That gives broad plaster and wood surfaces a uniformly fine-grained look. Add subtle, low-frequency stains or color variation to the generated maps, especially for walls and floors, while keeping the current procedural/offline approach.  
   **Risk:** Keep bump strength and contrast restrained; stronger high-frequency bump can make the simple geometry look noisy rather than worn.

These changes fit the existing authored-geometry approach and avoid introducing a heavy asset or post-processing pipeline.
